Vaccinate anyone who is between 9 months and 60 years of age, is not pregnant, and is traveling to an endemic area. B
Consider vaccination, weighing risks and benefits, for all pregnant patients, children 6 to 9 months old, and adults over 60 years at high risk of exposure. B
Care for those with yellow fever is supportive. B

background.definition: Yellow fever is a viral syndrome caused by a vector-borne Flavivirus transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, a daytime-biting mosquito. Ae. aegypti was once endemic in parts of the United States. In areas where the daytime-biting Ae. aegypti mosquito has been eliminated, yellow fever has also been eliminated.

list.listitem: There are an estimated 200,000 cases and 30,000 deaths, per year worldwide.
Vector-borne Flavivirus is endemic to South America and Africa.
Risk factors include recent travel to or residence in an endemic area and lack of adequate immunization.
Incubation period is of 3 to 6 days.

Three transmission cycles; urban and jungle are found. Jungle form is transmitted primarily among nonhuman primates by Aedes, Sabethes and Haemagogus spp vectors, with transmission to humans during encroachment into jungle forest canopy. Intermediate form occurs in Jungle bordering areas in Africa by Aedes spp that transmits back and forth from humans to non-human primates. Urban form is transmitted by Ae. aegypti mosquitos between humans.
Bloodborne transmission is also theoritically possible with transfusion or needlestick injuries.
Travel to some areas of the world requires documented proof of vaccination. Guidelines are available from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

A systematic review concluded that a single yellow fever vaccine confers sustained life-long protective immunity against yellow fever. Vaccination with single-dose live, attenuated 17D yellow fever vaccine 10 days prior to arrival is recommended for all nonpregnant persons aged between 9 months and 60 years and traveling to endemic areas (areas in Africa and South America). B

Consider vaccination, weighing risks and benefits, for all pregnant patients, children 6 to 9 months old, adults over 60 years, or those with asymptomatic HIV defined as moderate CD4 counts (200-500/mm3) at high risk of exposure (e.g., during an epidemic). B

Contraindications to vaccination include: age less than 6 months, thymus disorder with abnormal immune function, symptomatic HIV or HIV with CD4 count less than 200/mm3, primary immunodeficiencies, immune suppression, malignancy, or transplantation. B

Adverse events associated with vaccination include headache, myalgia, fever, and encephalitis (rare). Avoid giving yellow fever vaccine with other live-virus vaccines. Vaccination protection is likely lifelong, but revaccination is recommended every 10 years. B
Local suppression of Ae. aegypti mosquito in endemic areas has decreased the transmission rate of yellow fever.

Among over 38 million yellow fever vaccine administrations in Africa from 2007 to 2010, 3116 adverse events following immunization (AEFI) were documented, and among these 5% were classified as serious. The incidence per 100,000 vaccine doses administered was 8.2 of all AEFI's and 0.43 for any serious AEFI.
In an outbreak in the Congo during a vaccine shortage, use of a fractional dose of vaccine (0.1 ml which is one-fifth of the usual dose) was effective at inducing seroconversion.

This result was confirmed in a randomized, bouble-blind, non-inferiority trial that demonstrated the immunogenicity and safety of fractional doses of "all WHO-prequalified yellow fever vaccines were non-inferior to the standard doses".
Suspect yellow fever in a patient with febrile illness, myalgia, headache, and nausea and vomiting, particularly in case of recent travel to or residence in an endemic area. C
Period of remission followed by signs and symptoms of renal or hepatic failure should prompt laboratory investigation. C
The majority of patients with infections are believed to be asymptomatic.
Presenting symptoms typically include fever, headache, malaise, weakness, photophobia, lumbosacral and other joint pain, bradycardia, and nausea and vomiting. These normally last for 3 days.

This is followed by a 24-hour remission period and then development of jaundice, proteinuria, oliguria, cardiovascular instability, and hemorrhage. These symptoms occur as a result of liver and renal failure along with bleeding secondary to thrombocytopenia and clotting dysfuction.
Patients usually have no history of immunization, either live in or have traveled to an endemic area, and may report a recent mosquito bite.
Yellow fever symptoms are similar to those of other hemorrhagic fevers, although patients with yellow fever tend to have more severe hepatic involvement.
The choice of test should be based on availability, cost, and the time until the results are available.

Options for laboratory confirmation include viral culture of blood or tissue; identification of yellow fever antigen or nucleic acid in tissue using immunohistochemistry, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), or polymerase chain reaction; and identification of yellow fever-specific immunoglobulin M by ELISA with more than 4-fold increase in neutralizing antibody titers.
Suspect yellow fever in a patient with febrile illness, myalgia, headache, and nausea and vomiting, particularly in case of recent travel to or residence in an endemic area.
A period of remission followed by signs and symptoms of renal or hepatic failure should prompt laboratory investigation.
Consider antiviral therapy pending confirmation of yellow fever diagnosis because patients with other hemorrhagic fevers (but not yellow fever) may benefit.
Care is primarily supportive. B
Patients with severe illness require hospitalization and possibly dialysis. C
Treatment is primarily supportive. This includes oral or intravenous intake of fluids and rest. Rarely, dialysis or blood transfusion may be needed.

Research is ongoing, but no antiviral therapy has yet been confirmed effective in human trials. Sofosbuvir (FDA approved antiviral for Hepatitis C) has been shown to improve outcomes in animal models.

Ribavirin is used to treat other hemorrhagic fevers caused by arenaviridae and bunyaviridae. If tests specific for yellow fever are pending and other hemorrhagic fever viruses are in the differential diagnosis, consider initiating ribavirin therapy.
Depending on the severity of symptoms, the mortality rate is 20% to 50%. B
Patients who are 60 years and older may be at an increased risk for serious systemic adverse events from the vaccine.
Protective immunity of vaccine is not diminished in healthy elderly people.
Vaccine is believed to be safe for pregnant mothers; although not contraindicated, it is recommended only if travel to high-risk areas is unavoidable and if risks are outweighed by benefits.
A physician-written vaccination waiver letter is recommended if a patient decides against vaccination.
Nursing mothers can be vaccinated if traveling to high-risk areas, but breast milk transmission is unknown.

Yellow fever vaccine is recommended after the age of 9 months for those traveling to or living in endemic areas. US Food and Drug Administration recommends against vaccination for infants younger than 9 months because of concerns for encephalitis. No formal safety studies have been performed to date.

Vaccination can be considered between the ages of 6 and 9 months if an infant is traveling to an area where there is endemic or epidemic yellow fever; it is absolutely contraindicated in infants younger than 6 months of age.
